family.name: Unimog
family.verdict: A farm tractor that joined the army and never came home. Portal axles, locking diffs and a frame that twists like a pretzel make it close to unstoppable. It isn't quick, quiet or cheap to fix, and nobody who owns one cares.
intro: The Unimog began in 1946 as a 'Universal Motor Device for Agriculture'. Engineers Albert Friedrich, Heinrich Rößler and Hans Zabel developed it at Erhard & Söhne in Schwäbisch Gmünd, and Zabel shortened the project name to Unimog. It had all-wheel drive, differential locks and portal axles, yet could do 50 km/h. After a debut at the 1948 DLG fair, Gebrüder Boehringer built about 600 of the first series. Daimler-Benz then built it at Gaggenau until production moved to Wörth on 26 August 2002.

Armies wanted one too. The [[unimog/unimog-404|Unimog 404]], or Unimog S, arrived in the mid-1950s with petrol engines and a big cargo bed. Gaggenau built 64,242 of them up to 1980, more than any other Unimog series. The heavy series followed in 1974–75 with an angular cab and an eight-speed gearbox. Its best seller, the 435-series [[unimog/unimog-u1300l|U1300L]], became the Bundeswehr's 2-tonne truck and later the favorite base for expedition campers.

Most American examples of both are used imports, many of them ex-military. Both trucks are now well past the 25-year import threshold. Parts, manuals and know-how come from a few specialists and a busy international owner community.

page.title: Unimog U1300L (435)
page.verdict: The Bundeswehr's 2-tonne mule became the dream base for expedition campers: portal axles, lockers everywhere, 440 mm under the diffs and a cab like a phone box. It cruises at 50 mph and drinks gear oil, and it'll go places your other trucks won't.

paragraphs: The U1300L is what you get when Mercedes asks its farm-machinery department for an army truck. Under the square cab are coil-sprung portal axles, locking differentials, a cranked frame that twists over ruts, and an eight-speed gearbox that runs from 0.15 to 80 km/h. Gaggenau built 30,726 trucks in the 435 series from 1975 to 1993. More than 21,000 were U 1300 Ls, many of them for the Bundeswehr and German fire brigades. Today they come out of military surplus and into the hands of people building campers that can cross the Sahara. You won't do 70 mph, but you can drive almost anywhere.

story.heading: THE HEAVY SERIES
paragraphs: Daimler-Benz showed its new heavy series, the SBU, at the 1974 DLG exhibition. Its angular cab won the Federal Design Award, and Mercedes says the look still defines the Unimog today. The bigger change was underneath. More powerful engines needed a new drivetrain, and new noise rules meant the engine and gearbox were no longer bolted together. Gaggenau developed an eight-speed gearbox with double reduction, plus a crawler gear and power take-offs. The cranked U-section frame came from the Unimog S, the [[unimog/unimog-404|404]]. Mercedes says it gave excellent torsional flexibility off-road.

Production started in 1975 with the U 1300 and the long-wheelbase U 1300 L. The 435 used the 425's cab but had a longer 3,250 mm wheelbase and bigger engines. The U 1300 L got a 5.7-litre direct-injection six making 96 kW (130 PS) and 363 N·m; Mercedes' operator's manual calls it the OM 352. The turbocharged U 1700 L made 124 kW and 520 N·m and could carry up to 5 tonnes. From 1987 the 6.0-litre OM 366 replaced the older engine. Brakes are air-over-hydraulic discs, and the front axle, transfer case and lockers are all engaged with air.

story.heading: LKW 2 T TMIL GL
paragraphs: The Bundeswehr adopted the 435 in 1978 as the 'Lkw 2 t tmil gl', its second-generation standard utility truck, replacing the 1.5-tonne Unimog. About 18,000 were delivered. They served as troop and cargo carriers, engineer flatbeds, radio and field-office trucks, repair-crew vehicles and ambulances, and as tractors for 1.5-tonne trailers and towed weapons of up to 2.25 tonnes. Other NATO forces used them too, including US forces stationed in Germany.

Army spec explains a lot of what you'll find today. One Steel Soldiers member selling ex-US Army Europe trucks described them as 24-volt, with no hydraulic system and basic trim. Their contract plates let you trace a truck's service history. Military trucks were rated at 1,500 kg of payload on a 5,760 kg truck, with an 800 km range and a top speed of 80 km/h. Ex-Bundeswehr ambulances and cargo trucks, plus the odd ex-fire-brigade truck, turn up regularly at US auctions.

story.heading: SAND, CREW CABS AND CAMPERS
paragraphs: Civilian buyers found other uses. From 1983 Wackenhut of Nagold built crew cabs for the U 1300 L that seated up to seven, and Mercedes says they were popular for expeditions and research trips. In 1985 Karl-Friedrich Capito and his sons Jost and Volker won the truck class of the 14,000 km Paris–Dakar with converted U 1300 Ls. The rally trucks made 180 hp and had roll bars and six extra Hella lamps.

The camper scene picked it up from there. The 3,250 mm wheelbase takes a decent box, the portal axles give 440 mm of ground clearance, and the angles are 46 degrees in front and 51 at the rear. Plenty of builds end up too heavy, though. One HUBB contributor warns that many U1300L campers exceed the 7,500 kg gross weight once loaded for travel. Weigh the truck as you'll drive it, not as it's listed.

story.heading: SUCCESSION AND THE SURPLUS ERA
paragraphs: Mercedes rebuilt the Unimog range in 1988. The new heavy 437 series had the UG 3/65 gearbox and charge-air-cooled OM 366 A and LA engines, and stayed on sale until 2002. The 435 continued alongside it until 1993. Its successors are faster, quieter and more comfortable, and they cost more. They're also further from the simple, mechanical truck that owners like about the 435.

In the US the U1300L now sits between military surplus and a collector truck. Bring a Trailer has sold plain ex-army trucks for around $30,000 in 2026 and finished expedition campers for more than $170,000. It shares its portal-axle thinking with the [[hummer/h1|Hummer H1]] and the [[g-class/4x4-squared|G 500 4×4²]], and it was a Cold War contemporary of the [[pinzgauer/pinzgauer-710-712|Pinzgauer]]. It's slower than all three.

callout.label: SIDEBAR · PARIS–DAKAR 1985
callout.title: The Capito family's desert win
paragraphs: Karl-Friedrich Capito's team just missed the 1984 finish because of a minor defect. For 1985 their U 1300 L was fully overhauled at the Gaggenau factory. The rally truck made 180 hp and had a reinforced cab with roll bars and six extra 750-watt Hella headlamps.

Mercedes credits the coil-sprung axles and low weight for its speed across the scree desert. Its low height also got it through a jungle section faster than some rivals. Capito and his sons Jost and Volker won the truck competition over 14,000 km from Versailles to Dakar.

page.engineering_intro: The 435 is a heavy-series Unimog. It has a flexible cranked ladder frame and coil-sprung portal axles at both ends, and the eight-speed gearbox is mounted separately from the engine to cut noise and vibration. Compressed air does a lot of the work: it engages the front axle and the lockers, assists the clutch and actuates the hydraulic disc brakes. The engine is a mechanical, direct-injection Mercedes truck six with no electronics.

Gear reduction at each hub gives 440 mm of ground clearance

buying_checks.head: Portal hub oil level
buying_checks.body: Owners call the portals the key weak point. Oil can migrate out of a hub, the left front especially, and starve the bearings. Pull the fill and drain plugs on all four, check the level and look for metal on the magnet. Budget for bearings and seals if you find either problem (Iain_U1250, Expedition Portal).

buying_checks.head: Breather pumping and diff overfill
buying_checks.body: On 6-lug trucks like the U1300, the front portal breather hose can pump hub oil into the differential. Owners report the same thing at the rear. If a differential is overfull and a hub is low, that's the cause. Ask whether separate breathers or a vent fix have been fitted (m37charlie, HUBB; Hodakaguy, Expedition Portal).

buying_checks.head: Gearbox
buying_checks.body: A bad transmission can cost as much as the truck (gdict, Steel Soldiers), though one UK owner quotes gearbox rebuilds at about £5,000 (Pictish, HUBB). Drive it through all eight gears and both directions, cold and hot, and listen for grinding or jumping out of gear. If it ever needs a tow, go gently: one owner notes the gearbox oil pump sits high in the case.

buying_checks.head: Which engine is fitted
buying_checks.body: Check whether it's the naturally aspirated 5.7 OM 352, the turbo OM 352A or the 6.0 OM 366/366A. Filters, injector nozzles, water pumps and manuals all differ. Repowers and replacement turbos are common, so read the engine plate rather than trusting the ad.

buying_checks.head: Military spec vs civilian
buying_checks.body: Ex-army trucks are 24-volt and basically trimmed, and ex-US Army Europe trucks were described as having no hydraulic system (Steel Soldiers). Check for any PTO, hydraulic or crawler-gear equipment you need. Contract plates help trace a military truck's history.

buying_checks.head: Paint and rust
buying_checks.body: BaT listings for 435s have shown bubbling at the windshield base and on tailgates and bed hinges. Look under the cab mats and at the bed floor too. A fresh green respray can hide a lot.

buying_checks.head: Air system and brakes
buying_checks.body: The brakes, front axle engagement and lockers all depend on compressed air. Make sure the system builds pressure quickly and holds it overnight, that both lockers engage and release, and that the air dryer cartridge isn't years old. Soft brake-pad compounds chatter less than the factory pads, according to Expedition Imports.

buying_checks.head: Weight and registration
buying_checks.body: If it's a camper, weigh it. Many builds exceed the 7,500 kg gross weight. Check how the title describes the truck (truck, motorhome or exempt vehicle) and how your state registers a 7.5-tonne air-braked import before you pay.

repairs.title: Replace portal hub seals and fix the breathers
repairs.symptoms: A hub low on oil, or oil spraying on the inner wheel or dripping from the portal. On the front axle, a differential that's overfull while its hub is low means the breather is pumping oil across. If one hub runs hotter than its partner on an infrared check, investigate.
repairs.fix: Drain the portal and differential and note how much comes out. Remove the wheel and portal cover, then replace the lower outer hub seal and the upper input seal. Many 6-lug axles use a 140 mm lower seal, but late SBU axles take a different upper inner seal, so check your axle number first. Fit a new wear ring if the old one is grooved. Clear or separate the hub and diff breathers so the hub can't pump into the axle; some owners fit independent breathers or auxiliary reservoirs. Refill each portal with about 300 ml of GL-5 gear oil and the differential to its plug. Recheck the levels after a few hundred kilometres.
repairs.tools: Large sockets and breaker bar · seal driver · infrared thermometer · clean drain pan · 435 repair manual for torque values · seal numbers depend on axle serial

parts.name: SBU upper inner portal box seal, late (front axle from U011485, rear from U014896)
Lower outer portal hub seal, 140 mm (6-bolt diesel axles, incl. 1300)
Hub reduction wear ring 4353370851 (later axles incl. U1300L)

repairs.title: Rebuild a portal with new bearings
repairs.symptoms: Metal on the drain-plug magnet, a growl that changes with road speed, a hub that runs hot, or a hub that has been run low on oil. One Expedition Portal owner says U1300L portals weren't designed for constant 100 km/h running or larger tires.
repairs.fix: Strip the portal box following the 435 repair manual, then clean and inspect the gears and casing. Replace the bearings, seals and wear rings as a set. Some owners fit the stronger bearings from U1550L/SEE portals, with roller bearings in place of the ball bearings, but that needs matching gears and wear rings. Reassemble, refill with GL-5 gear oil and monitor the temperature against the other hubs for the first few drives. In an emergency, one owner reports filling a failed portal with grease to limp home.
repairs.tools: Full metric socket set · bearing puller and press · seal drivers · torque wrench · 435 repair manual

repairs.title: Replace disc brake pads
repairs.symptoms: Squeal or chatter, uneven or thin pads, or a pull under braking. One owner traced a rear portal running 70 °C to a sticking rear pad.
repairs.fix: Chock the truck and release the air system pressure as the manual describes. Support the axle and remove the wheel. Remove the pad retaining pins and springs and push the pistons back carefully, watching the fluid reservoir level. Clean the caliper, fit new pads, pins and springs, and check the pistons slide freely. A full truck takes three pad sets: the front axle has four calipers and the rear two. Bed the pads in gently.
repairs.tools: Wheel dolly or tire bar · piston spreader · brake cleaner · torque wrench

parts.name: Brake pad set, soft compound (6-lug axles incl. U1300L; 3 sets per truck)

repairs.title: Service the air dryer and drain the air tanks
repairs.symptoms: Water spitting from tank drains, slow pressure build, sluggish locker or front-drive engagement, or a dryer that purges constantly.
repairs.fix: Drain the air system completely. Unscrew the desiccant cartridge from the dryer, oil the new seal lightly and spin the new canister on hand-tight. Open each tank drain until only dry air comes out, and replace any drain valve that leaks or sticks. Run the engine, check how quickly pressure builds, and confirm the governor cuts out and the lockers engage.
repairs.tools: Strap wrench · soapy water for leak checks

parts.name: Desiccant air dryer canister (U1300L and others)

repairs.title: Replace the clutch master cylinder
repairs.symptoms: A pedal that sinks, a clutch that won't fully release, grinding into gear, or fluid on the footwell or firewall. Many trucks also have a clutch booster, so a heavy pedal can mean an air fault rather than a hydraulic one.
repairs.fix: Drain or siphon the reservoir. Disconnect the pushrod and hydraulic line, unbolt the master cylinder and fit the SBU replacement. Bleed the clutch at the slave or booster end until the fluid runs clear and bubble-free, then check the free play and full release with the engine running.
repairs.tools: Flare-nut wrenches · bleed hose and bottle · brake fluid to the manual's spec

repairs.title: Replace the water pump (OM 352)
repairs.symptoms: Coolant weeping from the pump's tell-tale hole, a wobbling pulley, bearing noise, or creeping temperature under load.
repairs.fix: Drain the coolant and remove the belts and fan. Unbolt the pump and clean the mating face. The Geba replacement for naturally aspirated U1300Ls (OM 353.960/.961/.962/.980) comes with its gasket. Refit, tension the belts, refill with the specified antifreeze, and bleed the system before a long run. OM 366 engines use a different pump.
repairs.tools: Metric sockets and wrenches · gasket scraper · belt tension gauge

repairs.title: Replace shock absorbers
repairs.symptoms: Bouncing after bumps, wallowing on the road, or leaking or rusted shocks. This is common on campers carrying more than the original spec.
repairs.fix: Support the chassis on stands, then unbolt and remove each shock, keeping track of spacers and bushings. Fit new shocks with new bushings. For a heavy camper, match the springs to the load too: Hellgeth makes 435-specific coils for heavy rear-axle loads.
repairs.tools: Jack and stands · metric sockets · penetrating oil

parts.name: Sachs OE heavy-duty shock absorber for U1300

repairs.title: Replace a head gasket (OM 352 / OM 366)
repairs.symptoms: Coolant loss with no visible leak, bubbles in the coolant, white exhaust smoke, or oil in the coolant.
repairs.fix: Drain the coolant and remove the intake, exhaust, injector lines and valve cover. Loosen the head bolts in the manual's sequence and lift the head. Have the head checked for flatness and cracks, then clean the deck. Fit the new gasket and new head bolts, which Expedition Imports strongly recommends, and torque them in stages to the 435 manual's sequence. Reset the valve clearances and refill and bleed the cooling system.
repairs.tools: Torque wrench and angle gauge · engine hoist or helper for the six-cylinder head · straight edge · 435 repair manual

parts.name: Cylinder head bolt set OM352 and OM366

baseline_service.intro: Most 435s in the US have spent years in a German army depot and then a container. Expect old fluids, aged tires and seals that have sat dry. Get the operator's manual for your engine first; Mercedes printed it in English. Then change every fluid before you drive it far, as one owner did before a 1,650 km trip home.

items.spec: Diesel engine oil to the operator's manual · capacity [CONFIRM IN MANUAL]
items.interval: Then at the manual's interval; owners drain the portals at the same time (about every 8,000 km)
items.note: Expedition Imports lists MANN filter 3661800809 for 435.115 U 1300 Ls with OM 353.961 (1978–1989) and OM 353.959 (from 1987). Check your filter housing before ordering.

items.spec: GL-5 hypoid gear oil, 75W-90 synthetic to MB sheet 235.8 suggested · about 300 ml per portal (≈ 1.2 L total)
items.note: Check all four for metal on the plug and compare the levels; a low hub plus an overfull diff points to breather pumping. Some owners also log hub temperatures.

parts.name: Lower outer portal seal, 140 mm (carry a spare)

items.spec: GL-5 gear oil (Mobil lists 75W-90 synthetic or 80W-90) · about 2.5 L each in Mobil's Unimog table
items.interval: Drain and refill on purchase, then per the manual
items.note: An overfull diff means a portal is pumping oil into it.

items.spec: Civilian: synthetic 75W-85 GL-4 to MB sheet 235.4 · Ex-Bundeswehr (BW 435): MB sheet 231.3 calls for 10W engine oil
items.note: Use GL-4, not GL-5 (m37charlie, BITOG). Check which spec your manual and gearbox tag call for, because the military 435 gearbox is the exception.

items.interval: On purchase, then per the manual; drain the tanks regularly
items.note: Moisture in the air system shortens the life of locker, front-drive and brake valves.

parts.name: Desiccant air dryer canister (U1300L and others)

items.spec: Replace the elements and pre-filter; drain the water
items.interval: On purchase, then per the manual
items.note: Stored trucks collect water and sediment in the tank. One ex-army truck on BaT had its fuel tank reconditioned and its filter replaced.

items.spec: Dry element (part number by engine; confirm in the parts manual)
items.interval: On purchase; check often in dust
items.note: Owners in dusty country add a cyclone pre-cleaner to the snorkel (Hodakaguy, Expedition Portal).

items.spec: MB-approved antifreeze · type and capacity [CONFIRM IN MANUAL]
items.note: Check the water pump weep hole and hoses while it's drained.

items.spec: Fluid to the manual · replace the reservoir filter
items.interval: Expedition Imports suggests every 3–5 years on other Unimog series
items.note: Expedition Imports calls the steering filter the most overlooked filter on a Unimog. Confirm the 435's filter part number in the parts manual.

items.spec: Brake fluid to the manual [CONFIRM IN MANUAL]
items.note: The brakes and the clutch are hydraulic, operated by air; old fluid corrodes the master and slave cylinders.

items.spec: Every nipple: kingpins, propshafts, pedal and gear linkages
items.note: Regular greasing and oil checks are most of the work, and they aren't difficult (Merv, HUBB).

items.spec: Check the DOT date code and the load rating against your real weight
items.note: One BaT seller flagged a truck's original Continentals for replacement because of age. Don't go small on load rating on a heavy camper.
Clean the grounds, load-test the batteries as a pair, and check the starter. A new Bosch 24 V starter costs about half as much as a Mercedes rebuilt unit, according to Expedition Imports.

faq.q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
faq.a: Most U1300Ls in the US run 20-inch Continental MPT 81s or Michelin XZLs in 335/80R20 (12.5R20, about 40.6 in tall) or 365/80R20 (14.5R20, about 42.9 in), and several BaT trucks wear 365/80R20 MPT 81s. One builder chose 365s with fast axles to keep first gear low enough for trails. A 395/85R20 is too big for a U1300 without a cab lift, according to one Expedition Portal member, and it also loads the portal bearings, which are expensive.

faq.q: How fast will it go on the highway?
faq.a: The Bundeswehr quotes 80 km/h (50 mph). Depending on gearbox and portal ratios, top speed runs from 80 to 110 km/h. Owners say fast axles alone aren't enough: one says a fast-axle truck without an overdrive turns about 3,000 rpm at 70 mph, while another says fast axles manage 60 mph. A U1700 camper on 395s held about 55 mph. Cruising at around 65 km/h is more typical with a loaded camper.

faq.q: What fuel economy should I expect?
faq.a: Wikipedia gives 17.5–19 L/100 km (about 12–13 mpg US) for the U 1300 L. In practice, one owner averages about 11 mpg and another estimates 20–30 L/100 km (8–12 mpg) for a loaded truck, more in sand. Military range was 800 km.

faq.q: Why do the hubs lose oil?
faq.a: At sustained speed the portal gears can pump oil out through the breather, and on 6-lug axles like the U1300's, the front breather hose can feed hub oil into the differential. The fixes owners use are separate breathers or a vent fix, auxiliary reservoirs, new inner seals, and draining and refilling the portals (about 300 ml each) at every oil change. Some owners say the problem is overblown, citing hubs past 300,000 miles with one seal change.

faq.q: What oil goes in the gearbox?
faq.a: Mobil's table for U1000–U1700 transmissions lists a synthetic 75W-85 to MB sheet 235.4, and owners stress GL-4, not GL-5. The ex-Bundeswehr 'BW 435' is the exception: MB sheet 231.3 calls for 10W engine oil in that gearbox. Use GL-5 75W-90 in the differentials and portals.

The U 1700 L has a 124 kW turbo engine with 520 N·m against the base U 1300 L's 96 kW and 363 N·m. It sits on 10-lug axles, which one owner says don't suffer the breather-pumping problem of the 6-lug U1300. Another owner understood the U1700L to have reinforced axles and redesigned hubs, but says that's his reading of the sources rather than a verified fact. The U1300L was built in far greater numbers: 21,775 against 808 U 1700 Ls.

The OM 366 replaced the older engine from 1987. The two share head bolts and head gaskets. Turbo OM 352A and OM 366A engines use their own injector nozzles. Owners who want 60–65 mph with a camper talk about an OM 366 turbo with an intercooler and fuel tuning, at around 200 hp.

faq.q: Can I legally import and register one?
faq.a: Every 435 is now past the US 25-year exemption: the last were built in 1993. BaT trucks carry clean titles from states including Montana, Washington and Mississippi. Registration rules still vary by state, so check how yours titles a 7.5-tonne truck before you buy. See the import section below for sources.

faq.q: How much can it carry and tow?
faq.a: As the Bundeswehr's Lkw 2 t tmil gl it was rated for 1,500 kg of payload and towed 1.5-tonne trailers or weapons of up to 2.25 tonnes. Gross weight is 7,500 kg, so weigh a camper conversion: many end up over the limit.

faq.q: Is it a good overland camper base?
faq.a: For rough country, yes, but owners agree it's slow and noisy on tarmac and struggles in fast traffic. They recommend heavy sound insulation, air conditioning and better seats for ex-military trucks. A Vario or a MAN costs less if you don't need the Unimog's off-road ability.

mods.why: Campers carry far more weight on the rear axle than an army cargo truck. Hellgeth's 435-specific coils are rated for about 6,500 kg empty weight with a high rear-axle load, and stiffened against body roll.

who.name: Hellgeth — Unimog 1300L coil springs (via Expedition Imports)

mods.why: Adjustable KONI shocks developed with Hellgeth let you set rebound for the axle load. Sachs heavy-duty OE replacements cover the U1300.

who.name: Sachs HD shock absorber for U1300 (Expedition Imports)

mods.why: Two-piece bolt-together rims let you change a tire without heavy tools and run very low pressures in sand. Hellgeth makes a 6-bolt 20x11 rim.
The MPT 81 is the usual mixed-use choice: quiet, good in sand, snow and rock, but slow to clean out in deep mud, where an MPT 80 is better. Both are rated to 68 mph.
Ex-military trucks often need fenders, badging, keys and the civilian ignition bits. US Unimog specialists stock them.
